name: Isolated GnRH deficiency (normosmic idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism)

clinicalPearls: Characterised by absent or incomplete puberty due to deficient hypothalamic GnRH secretion or action, with low sex steroids and inappropriately low or normal gonadotropins (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism)

The normosmic form has a preserved sense of smell, distinguishing it from Kallmann syndrome, in which GnRH deficiency is accompanied by anosmia or hyposmia from defective olfactory-GnRH neuronal migration
The 'fertile eunuch' variant is a partial form in which limited gonadotropin secretion supports some spermatogenesis and testicular growth despite inadequate virilisation
In boys it may present in infancy with micropenis and cryptorchidism, reflecting the absent activity of the reproductive axis during the neonatal minipuberty
It is caused by mutations in genes governing GnRH neuron function and signalling (for example GNRHR, GNRH1, KISS1R, and TAC3/TACR3), with variable inheritance and incomplete penetrance
The chief diagnostic difficulty is distinguishing it from constitutional delay of growth and puberty, since both present with low gonadotropins before puberty
Management uses sex-steroid replacement to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, with gonadotropin therapy or pulsatile GnRH used to achieve fertility
Reversal of the hypogonadotropic state occurs in a minority, so periodic reassessment off treatment is warranted
reference.pathophysiology: Isolated GnRH deficiency arises from failure of the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator, either from deficient GnRH synthesis or secretion or from defective signalling at the pituitary GnRH receptor. Without adequate pulsatile GnRH stimulation, the pituitary secretes insufficient LH and FSH, so the gonads are not driven to produce sex steroids or gametes, resulting in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with absent or arrested puberty. In the normosmic form the olfactory system develops normally, unlike Kallmann syndrome where a shared developmental defect impairs migration of both olfactory and GnRH neurons. Numerous causative genes affect GnRH neuronal function, the kisspeptin and neurokinin B signalling pathways, and receptor activity, and the incomplete penetrance and occasional later reversibility indicate that the defect is one of axis regulation rather than fixed structural loss.
additionalDifferentials: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Functional hypogonadotropism from chronic illness, undernutrition, or excessive exercise
Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism from primary gonadal failure
additionalInvestigations: Basal LH, FSH, and sex-steroid levels (all low or inappropriately normal)
Formal assessment of olfaction to separate normosmic disease from Kallmann syndrome
Magnetic resonance imaging of the hypothalamus, pituitary, and olfactory structures
Anterior pituitary hormone profile to confirm the deficiency is isolated
Genetic testing of GnRH-axis genes and assessment for associated non-reproductive features
redFlags: Neonatal micropenis with bilateral cryptorchidism, which should prompt early endocrine evaluation
Visual field defects, headache, or other pituitary hormone deficiencies suggesting an intracranial mass
Associated midline or skeletal anomalies indicating a syndromic cause
Complete absence of pubertal onset well beyond the normal age range
reference.prognosis: Secondary sexual development and, in many cases, fertility can be achieved with appropriate hormonal and gonadotropin therapy; a subset of patients experience reversal of the deficiency, but untreated disease leaves patients hypogonadal with associated bone loss and infertility.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with constitutional delay, since the two are biochemically similar before puberty and only time or careful testing distinguishes them
Failing to test smell, thereby missing the distinction between normosmic disease and Kallmann syndrome
Assuming the deficiency is permanent and not reassessing for the possibility of reversal
Overlooking neonatal signs (micropenis, cryptorchidism) that offer an early diagnostic clue
Not screening for other pituitary deficits before concluding the defect is isolated
management: Sex-steroid replacement, testosterone in males and staged oestrogen then combined oestrogen-progestogen in females, to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics
Gonadotropin therapy or pulsatile GnRH to stimulate spermatogenesis or ovulation when fertility is desired
Specialist-directed short-course androgen or gonadotropin therapy in infant boys with micropenis or cryptorchidism
Bone-health optimisation through adequate sex-steroid replacement, calcium and vitamin D, with monitoring of bone mineral density to counter hypogonadal bone loss
Periodic reassessment for spontaneous reversal of the deficiency, and careful distinction from constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Genetic counselling given the identified GnRH-axis gene defects and their variable inheritance and penetrance
Reproductive and paediatric endocrinology referral for puberty induction and fertility planning
